facts.text: On this date in 1485, the Battle of Bosworth Field ended the Plantagenet dynasty after 331 years — the last English king to die in battle fell in a muddy Leicestershire field, and his bones turned up under a parking lot in 2012.
On this date in 1864, twelve nations signed the first Geneva Convention, creating the red cross emblem on the spot — Switzerland's flag, simply inverted.
More people live inside a circle drawn 4,000 km around Bangladesh than outside it — that single radius captures over half of all humanity.
Canada has more lakes than every other country on Earth combined, yet its entire population fits comfortably inside Tokyo's greater metro area.
The city of Ilfracombe, England, sits at a higher latitude than parts of Labrador, Canada — the Gulf Stream, not geography, explains why Britain grows palm trees.
On this day in 1987, the Dow fell 4.8% — the opening shot of a two-month slide that ended in Black Monday, the largest single-day percentage crash in Wall Street history.

On this day in 1642, England's King Charles I declared war on Parliament. The resulting civil war so disrupted trade that London's goldsmith-bankers invented deposit receipts — the prototype of modern paper money.
The S&P 500 has historically returned more in the four months after a 20% drawdown than in any equivalent bull-market period. Fear, it turns out, is the market's most reliable sale sign.
Berkshire Hathaway's 'A' shares have never been split. At roughly $700,000 each, a single share costs more than the median American house — by design: Buffett wanted owners, not traders.
The entire global bond market is roughly four times the size of the global stock market. Equities get the headlines; debt runs the world.

On this date in 1963, the X-15 aircraft reached 354,200 feet — officially crossing into space. Its pilot, Joseph Walker, became an astronaut without ever leaving Earth's atmosphere by NASA's own definition.

On this date in 1485, the Battle of Bosworth ended the Plantagenet dynasty. The last king to die in battle on English soil, Richard III, was found centuries later under a Leicester parking lot with his hands still bound.
Your bones are constantly dissolving and rebuilding themselves. Every decade, you replace nearly your entire skeleton — the femur you have now did not exist ten years ago.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A single teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh roughly a billion tons on Earth.

Tardigrades can survive open space. Exposed to vacuum, radiation, and temperature extremes in low Earth orbit, a significant portion returned alive — making them the only animals confirmed to endure unshielded spaceflight.
On this day in 1485, Richard III died at Bosworth Field — ending the Plantagenet dynasty that had ruled England for 331 years, longer than the United States has existed.
Oxford University was teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. Oxford dates to 1096; Tenochtitlan wasn't founded until 1325.
On this day in 1864, twelve nations signed the first Geneva Convention — the same week Ulysses Grant was mired in the Siege of Petersburg, with no end in sight.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. She died in 30 BC; the pyramid rose around 2560 BC.
The fax machine was patented in 1843 — before the American Civil War, before the telephone, and a full 146 years before Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web.
Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012. Now it belongs to the language.
Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh longing for a home that no longer exists, or perhaps never did. Untranslatable into English, which says something about what English has chosen not to feel.
On this day in 1485, Richard III died at Bosworth Field. The word 'henchman' once meant a groom who walked beside a horse — his loyal attendants made the word mean something darker.
Meraki (v./adv.): Greek for doing something with soul, creativity, and love — leaving a piece of yourself in the work. The Greeks had a word for it. Most managers do not.

On this day in 1902, Cadillac was founded. The marque descends from Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac — whose name came from a French village whose name came from 'cadat,' meaning chief. Prestige is layered.
On this date in 2012, Coinbase officially launched to the public, offering Bitcoin purchases at $10.28 per coin. It would later IPO at a $65.3B valuation — the largest U.S. exchange debut in history.

On August 22, 2017, Bitcoin's mempool cleared almost entirely following the SegWit activation lock-in, briefly dropping average fees to under $0.10 — a calm before the December 2017 fee storm hit $50+ per transaction.
The Bitcoin genesis block contains the headline 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' — Satoshi embedded it as a timestamp and a pointed editorial, not just a curiosity.
Ethereum's EIP-1559, activated in August 2021, has since burned over 4 million ETH permanently. The fee-burning mechanism turned ETH into a deflationary asset during periods of high network demand.

The DAO hack of 2016 drained 3.6M ETH through a reentrancy bug — but the attacker was partially bound by a 28-day time-lock, giving Ethereum developers the window they needed to execute the controversial hard fork.

On this date in 2012, Google's 'cat neuron' paper was published — a neural net trained on unlabeled YouTube frames spontaneously developed a neuron selective for cat faces, without ever being told cats existed.

On this date in 1956, the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence entered its third month — the workshop that coined 'artificial intelligence' as a field attracted fewer than 10 participants and produced no consensus results.

AlphaFold2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins — essentially the entire known proteome of life on Earth — in roughly 12 months of GPU time, a task estimated to take structural biology centuries by hand.

GPT-4's training run is estimated to have consumed around 50 gigawatt-hours of electricity, comparable to the annual consumption of roughly 4,500 average US households, all to produce a single set of weights.
The first neural network to defeat a professional human player at Go, AlphaGo, was trained partly against itself — its strongest opponent during training was a version of itself from the future.
